anarchism: Anarchism is the political view that societies can and should be organized without coercive, top-down authority. Many anarchists do not oppose organization or even rules, but insist that every hierarchy must justify itself or be dismantled in favor of voluntary cooperation, mutual aid, and self-governance. On this view, anarchism is a vision of ordered freedom, not mere chaos.
aquinas-five-ways: The Five Ways are Thomas Aquinas's five arguments, in his Summa Theologiae, that God exists. Each starts from an ordinary feature of the world — motion, causes, contingency, degrees of perfection, purposes — and argues that it points to a first mover or necessary being. They remain among the most discussed arguments for God, though Hume, Kant, and later critics challenged each step.
banality-of-evil: The banality of evil is Hannah Arendt's phrase, coined at the 1961 trial of Adolf Eichmann, for the thought that terrible wrongs are often done not by monsters but by ordinary officials who fail to think about what they are doing. On her account, thoughtlessness — an inability to see the deed from another's standpoint — lets routine functionaries take part in atrocity. The idea remains influential and contested.
chinese-room: The Chinese Room is John Searle's thought experiment against the claim that running the right program is enough for a mind. A person who understands no Chinese follows rulebooks for matching Chinese symbols, producing answers that convince outsiders he is fluent — yet he grasps nothing. Searle concludes that symbol manipulation can yield behavior without genuine understanding; a famous reply holds that the whole system, not the person, understands.
climate-ethics: Climate ethics asks what we owe to one another, to future generations, and to the natural world in the face of human-caused climate change. It grapples with the problem's unusual structure: emissions are spread across billions of people, harms fall hardest on those least responsible, and the worst effects land decades away. Questions of justice, responsibility, and what a good life may cost the planet sit at its center.
ethics-of-belief: The ethics of belief holds that believing is something we can be praised or blamed for. In an 1877 essay, W. K. Clifford argued that it is always wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence, telling of a ship-owner who silences his doubts and sends an unseaworthy ship to sea. William James famously replied that some commitments are too vital to wait for proof.
functionalism: Functionalism is a leading theory of mind on which a mental state — pain, belief, desire — is defined by what it does, not what it is made of: its causes, effects, and relations to other states. If so, minds need not be built from neurons; anything playing the right causal roles, silicon included, could realize one. This openness to non-biological minds makes functionalism central to debates about artificial intelligence.
i-thou: The I–Thou relation is Martin Buber's account of the deepest way of meeting another: encountering a person — or, for Buber, God — as a full subject, whole and unreduced, in mutual dialogue. Its opposite is the I–It stance, where we treat others as objects to use or analyze from a distance. For Buber, real living happens in meeting, though life constantly pulls us back toward treating people as Its.
informal-fallacies: Informal fallacies are common patterns of bad reasoning identified by content and context rather than broken logical form — attacking the arguer instead of the argument (ad hominem), misrepresenting a position to knock it down (straw man), or treating a contested chain of consequences as inevitable (slippery slope). Naming them sharpens everyday argument, though accusations of fallacy can themselves be misapplied, since a suspect-looking move is sometimes legitimate.
justice-as-fairness: Justice as fairness is John Rawls's theory, presented in A Theory of Justice (1971): the principles governing a society should be ones its members would choose from a fair starting point, behind a 'veil of ignorance' hiding their own class, talents, and beliefs. Rawls argues this yields equal basic liberties for all, plus the rule that inequalities are permissible only when they improve the position of the worst off.
locke-labor-property: The labor theory of property is John Locke's account of how private property arises legitimately: when a person mixes their labor with unowned resources, they gain a right to the result, since the work is theirs. Locke attached limits — leave 'enough and as good' for others, and do not let things spoil. Many later arguments about property build on the theory, though critics question whether labor works this way.
maslow-hierarchy-of-needs: Maslow's hierarchy of needs is Abraham Maslow's proposal that human motivation is organized in levels: we generally secure physiological needs and safety before belonging, esteem, and finally self-actualization — becoming all we can be — become our driving concerns. Though widely taught and intuitively appealing, the strict ordering has been empirically questioned, and the model survives more as a flexible picture of what people need than as a rigid law.
nagarjuna-emptiness: Emptiness (shunyata) is the central teaching of the Buddhist philosopher Nagarjuna: nothing possesses its own independent, fixed essence. Everything exists only through dependence — on causes, parts, and the concepts by which we grasp it — like a chariot that is nothing over and above its parts arranged in a certain way. Nagarjuna insisted emptiness is not nihilism; seeing it loosens the clinging that generates suffering.
narrative-identity: Narrative identity is the idea that we make sense of who we are by shaping our lives into stories — selecting events, finding connections, and casting ourselves as characters whose actions follow from a developing plot. Thinkers such as Alasdair MacIntyre and Paul Ricoeur hold that this storytelling is not decoration but partly constitutive of the self. Critics counter that some selves, and some lives, resist narrative form altogether.
one-dimensional-man: One-Dimensional Man is Herbert Marcuse's 1964 diagnosis of advanced industrial society: by delivering comfort and consumption, it absorbs the very forces that once criticized it, leaving people with needs shaped by advertising and a rationality devoted only to means, never to ends. Opposition does not disappear but gets sold back as another lifestyle. The book became a touchstone of 1960s radical critique of consumer capitalism.
open-society: The open society is Karl Popper's ideal of a community that expects its beliefs and institutions to be fallible and correctable through free criticism, open debate, and peaceful change of government. Its opposite is the closed society, ruled by dogma, taboo, or an infallible authority. For Popper this ideal grows from how knowledge itself advances — by trial and error — and even tolerance has limits when intolerance exploits it.
prisoners-dilemma: The prisoner's dilemma is a game-theory puzzle: two suspects who cannot coordinate each do best by betraying the other, whatever the other does, yet if both betray, both end up worse than if both had stayed loyal. It captures how individually rational choices can produce collectively bad outcomes. The strategy tit-for-tat — cooperate first, then mirror your partner's last move — showed cooperation can emerge when the game is repeated.
private-language: The private language argument is Wittgenstein's challenge to the idea that a person could have a meaningful language only they could, in principle, understand — say, private words for inner sensations. His later philosophy holds that meaning requires public standards: rules one can follow correctly or incorrectly only against shared practice. On this view there can be no purely private language, a claim that reshaped philosophy of mind.
problem-of-other-minds: The problem of other minds asks how we can know that anyone besides ourselves has a mind — that behind outward faces there is real experience rather than unfeeling machines. I have direct access to my own pain but only to others' outward signs. Proposed answers range from analogy to treating belief in other minds as the best explanation of behavior; some argue the question dissolves once language is understood.
reid-common-sense: Common sense philosophy is Thomas Reid's Scottish Enlightenment response to Humean skepticism. Reid argued that certain first principles — that the senses give real information, that memory is generally trustworthy, that people usually mean what they say — are part of our constitution, reasonable to trust without proof; denying them leads to absurdity, not wisdom. He also held that we perceive objects directly, not just inner images of them.
reliabilism: Reliabilism is a theory of knowledge on which a belief counts as justified, or knowledge, when produced by a process that reliably delivers truth — good eyesight, careful reasoning, trustworthy memory. What matters is the actual reliability of the process, not whether the believer can argue for it. This externalist turn handles puzzles about luck in knowledge, though critics design cases where a reliable method still yields an unearned verdict.
searle-intentionality: Biological naturalism is John Searle's view that consciousness and intentionality — the 'aboutness' of thoughts, the way a belief is about Paris — are genuine biological features of brains, as physical as digestion. Mental states are caused by brain processes while remaining irreducible to them. Searle insists computation alone cannot produce them: a program manipulates symbols without caring what they mean.
situationism: Situationism, in ethics, is a challenge from social psychology to the idea of stable character. Studies such as Milgram's obedience experiments and the hurried-seminarian study suggest that small situational pressures — an authority present, being late — predict behavior better than presumed virtues or vices do. If so, the ideal of firmly good character may be empirically shaky, one many philosophers accept only partially, arguing character survives in weakened form.
wilderness-ethics: Wilderness and nature aesthetics explore the value of untamed nature. Wilderness ethics asks whether wild places matter only for human use — resources, recreation — or possess worth of their own that grounds duties of preservation. Nature aesthetics studies what makes an experience of forest, landscape, or storm genuine appreciation rather than scenic consumption. Both traditions feed a broader question: what we owe to places we did not make.
